title: Design YouTube (upload, transcoding, streaming)
scopeHtml: Scope: resumable upload, transcoding DAG, adaptive bitrate streaming, CDN, metadata.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
YouTube lets creators upload videos and lets anyone stream them smoothly on any device and network. Netflix, Hotstar and Vimeo share the same core: ingest a huge file, convert it into many formats, and deliver small pieces through a CDN. This note covers upload, transcoding and streaming.

Functional requirements

  • Upload a video (up to several GB), with title, description, thumbnail.
  • The system processes it into multiple resolutions and formats.
  • Watch a video with adaptive quality (480p on a weak network, 4K on a strong one); seek anywhere.
  • Basic metadata: views, likes, search by title (out of scope here but mentioned).

Non-functional requirements

  • Playback starts in under 2 s (time to first frame), very little rebuffering.
  • Uploads are resumable (mobile networks drop).
  • Highly available playback (99.99%); processing can lag minutes to hours.
  • Scale: 500 hours of video uploaded per minute (YouTube's publicly cited figure), 1B hours watched per day, strongly read-heavy.

Decision gravity. Choose adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS or MPEG-DASH) over serving one big MP4. It costs a transcoding pipeline and many stored copies but removes buffering for users on bad networks. This is a one-way door at the format level: players, DRM and CDN caching rules all depend on it. Netflix and YouTube both use it.

Everyday analogy. A bakery that bakes one loaf, then slices it into thin, medium and thick slices so every customer can take what they can chew.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing to stream a single file from your app server.
  • Forgetting resumable uploads.
  • Not separating the upload/processing path from the (much bigger) playback path.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/videos                      // step 1: create metadata, get an upload session
{ "title": "My trip", "description": "...", "sizeBytes": 2147483648, "contentType": "video/mp4" }
201 { "videoId": "v_8Hq2", "uploadUrl": "https://up.yt.com/u/sess_91", "chunkSize": 8388608 }
PUT https://up.yt.com/u/sess_91     // step 2: upload chunks, resumable
Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/2147483648
308 Resume Incomplete   Range: bytes=0-8388607
...
200 OK                   (last chunk)  { "videoId": "v_8Hq2", "status": "PROCESSING" }

HEAD/PUT with Content-Range: bytes */2147483648   -> returns how many bytes the server has (resume)
GET /v1/videos/v_8Hq2
200 { "videoId":"v_8Hq2", "status":"READY", "title":"My trip", "durationSec": 612,
      "manifestUrl": "https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/master.m3u8",
      "thumbnailUrl": "https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/thumb.jpg", "views": 15234 }
GET https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/master.m3u8     // HLS master playlist
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8

GET https://cdn.yt.com/v_8Hq2/1080p/seg_00042.ts    // 4-6 s segment, cacheable forever

Status moves UPLOADING -> PROCESSING -> READY | FAILED. This resumable protocol resembles the Google Cloud Storage resumable upload and tus.io; confirm exact header details in their docs.

Industry example. YouTube Data API uses resumable uploads; Netflix and Twitch publish HLS/DASH manifests.

Everyday analogy. A courier who gives you a tracking number, accepts the parcel in several trips, and tells you where he stopped if the van breaks down.

Common interview traps.

  • Uploading through the app server instead of directly to object storage using a pre-signed/session URL.
  • One giant PUT with no resume.
  • Serving video bytes through the API gateway.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 500 hours uploaded per minute, average source 1080p at 8 Mbps, 1B hours watched per day.

Quantity Calculation Result
Upload per day 500 h x 60 x 24 = 720,000 h/day 720k hours of video
Raw size 8 Mbps = 1 MB/s = 3.6 GB/hour; x 720k ~2.6 PB / day raw
Encoded ladder 144p..4K ladder totals ~ 1.5-2x the source size ~4-5 PB / day stored (before dedupe/cold tiering)
Upload bandwidth 2.6 PB / 86,400 s ~30 GB/s ingest = 240 Gbit/s
Transcode work 1 CPU-core encodes 1080p at ~0.5-1x realtime; a ladder ~5x work 720k h x 5 / 24 / 0.75 = ~200k cores continuously (hardware encoders reduce this a lot)
Playback bandwidth 1B hours x 3.6 GB (at avg 4 Mbps = 1.8 GB/h) = 1.8 EB/day ~21 TB/s average, ~100+ Tbit/s globally
Segment request rate 6 s segments, ~170M concurrent viewers ~28M segment requests/s

Takeaways: ingest and transcode are big but bounded; playback egress dwarfs everything and is why CDNs and ISP-embedded caches (Google Global Cache, Netflix Open Connect) exist.

Industry example. Netflix's Open Connect puts appliances inside ISPs; most of its traffic is served without leaving the ISP's network.

Everyday analogy. Making the bread is a night job for a few bakers; delivering it to a billion breakfast tables is the real logistics problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up bits and bytes (Mbps vs MB/s).
  • Skipping egress, the largest cost line.
  • Not saying that most videos are rarely watched (long tail), so cold storage tiers pay off.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components:

  • Upload service: issues resumable session URLs; chunks go straight to object storage (S3/GCS), multipart upload with 8 MB parts.
  • Metadata DB: Vitess/MySQL (YouTube used MySQL with Vitess) or Spanner/DynamoDB; video id, owner, status, rendition list.
  • Queue: Kafka/SQS; one message per video per task.
  • Transcoding workers: stateless pool using FFmpeg or hardware encoders; run as a DAG of tasks.
  • Processed store: object storage with segments plus manifests.
  • CDN: edge caches, then regional/origin shield, then origin.
  • Player: reads the manifest, picks a rendition by measured throughput.

Decision gravity: direct-to-storage upload. App servers stay light (they only mint URLs and track state). Alternative: proxy bytes through your servers; costs CPU, bandwidth and breaks at scale. Reversible.

Decision gravity: split video into segments (GOP-aligned 2-6 s chunks). It enables parallel transcoding, adaptive switching and CDN caching of small objects. A one-way door in practice since players and caches key on segment layout.

Industry examples. YouTube's published architecture (Vitess, Borg, Colossus) and Netflix's pipeline (the "Cosmos" platform and per-title encoding) follow this split.

Everyday analogy. A film lab: negatives come in through a loading dock, get duplicated in several sizes in the back, and finished prints go to local cinemas, not the lab.

Common interview traps.

  • A single monolithic transcode job per video (slow and not restartable).
  • Making the viewer wait until all renditions finish (publish lowest rendition first).
  • Treating the DB as the thing that stores video bytes.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Resumable, chunked upload

The session stores {videoId, totalSize, receivedBytes, uploadId} in Redis/DB with a 7-day TTL. Chunk 8 MB: smaller means more requests, larger means more resend on failure. S3 multipart allows up to 10,000 parts, 5 MB to 5 GB each; verify each part's checksum (MD5/CRC32C) and assemble on completion. Abandoned uploads are cleaned by a lifecycle rule after 7 days. Decision: chunk size is reversible per session.

Transcoding pipeline as a DAG

Steps: validate (reject corrupt files, virus/policy scan), split at keyframes, encode each chunk in parallel across hundreds of workers, then package into HLS/DASH segments with H.264 (universal), VP9/AV1 (smaller, slower), and AAC/Opus audio. A 10-minute video can finish in under a minute when split into 100 chunks. Idempotent tasks keyed by (videoId, rendition, chunk) so retries are safe. Priority queues: popular creators or livestream VODs first. Netflix uses per-title/per-shot encoding to pick the best bitrate ladder for each title, saving 20%+ bandwidth by their own reports.

Decision gravity: which codecs? H.264 everywhere, AV1 for popular videos only (encode cost is high but egress savings repay it when a video gets millions of views). This is reversible: you can add renditions later, though storing both costs space.

Adaptive bitrate streaming

The manifest lists renditions; the player downloads segment N at the quality its recent throughput supports (buffer-based and throughput-based algorithms), switching at segment boundaries. Typical ladder:

rendition  resolution  video bitrate
144p       256x144     0.1 Mbps
360p       640x360     0.8 Mbps
720p       1280x720    2.5 Mbps
1080p      1920x1080   5 Mbps
4K         3840x2160   16 Mbps

Segments are immutable and named by content, so the CDN can cache them for a year (Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable). Manifests for finished videos are cacheable too; live manifests need a 2-6 s TTL.

CDN strategy and the long tail

Popular 5% of videos produce most of the traffic: keep them at the edge. Long-tail videos fall through to regional caches or origin. Pre-position (push) new releases from popular channels. Hit ratio target above 95% at the edge; each 1% miss at 100 Tbit/s is still 1 Tbit/s hitting regional tiers. Cold content (no views in 90 days) moves to cheaper storage classes (S3 Infrequent Access/Glacier-like tiers), keeping only the lowest renditions hot and re-transcoding on demand.

Metadata, views and thumbnails

Metadata reads are cached (Redis, TTL 5 min). View counts: do not do UPDATE views = views + 1 per play. Batch increments through Kafka and aggregate every few seconds; show approximate counts (YouTube historically froze at "301 views" while validating). Thumbnails: extract a few frames, store as small JPEGs/WebP on the CDN.

Start-up latency and seek

Start with the lowest rendition for the first 1-2 segments then step up. Seek works by jumping to the segment containing the timestamp (index from the playlist). Smaller first segment (2 s) reduces time to first frame. Pre-connect TLS/DNS to the CDN.

Failure handling and DRM

Worker dies: queue visibility timeout re-delivers the task. Poison video: after 3 failures mark FAILED and notify the creator. DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady) is added at packaging with encrypted segments (CENC) and a license server; it only matters for premium content.

Production incident patterns. (1) A viral video's segments are cold in a new region: origin gets a thundering herd; fix with request coalescing at the origin shield. Metric: origin egress and cache hit ratio. (2) Transcoding queue backs up after a big upload wave: watch queue age, autoscale on it, and prioritise short videos. (3) Rebuffer ratio rising: track client-reported rebuffer %, per ISP.

Industry examples. YouTube (Vitess, Google Global Cache), Netflix (Open Connect, per-title encoding), Twitch (HLS with 2 s segments for lower latency).

Everyday analogy. A newspaper printing plant: the master page is cut into sections printed in parallel and trucked to local depots before breakfast.

Common interview traps.

  • A single transcoder queue with no parallelism within a video.
  • Updating view counts synchronously in the SQL row.
  • Ignoring the cache-hit-ratio math at CDN scale.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Separation of upload, processing and playback paths, and why each scales differently.
  • Direct-to-object-store resumable uploads.
  • Chunked parallel transcoding and an adaptive bitrate ladder (HLS/DASH).
  • CDN hierarchy, hit-ratio reasoning, cold-storage tiering.
  • Numbers: petabytes per day, egress in Tbit/s, cores for transcoding.
  • Trade-offs: codec choice vs encode cost, segment length vs latency, eventual counts.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Upload straight to object storage with resumable chunked sessions; app servers handle metadata only.
  • Transcode asynchronously: split into GOP chunks, encode in parallel into a ladder, package as HLS/DASH.
  • Players adapt quality per segment; segments are immutable and cached for a year on the CDN.
  • Egress, not storage or compute, is the dominant cost; edge caches and ISP appliances fix it.
  • Metadata in a sharded SQL or KV store with cache; counts via batched async aggregation.
  • Retries are safe because tasks are idempotent; poison videos go to FAILED.
  • Hard-to-change choices: segment layout, manifest format, DB sharding key.

questions.promptHtml: Why don't video platforms just serve one MP4 file? What is adaptive bitrate streaming and how does a player use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand the playback path and why transcoding exists at all.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One big file forces every viewer to the same quality: too heavy for a weak network, wasteful on a strong one. With adaptive bitrate (HLS or MPEG-DASH) the platform transcodes each video into a ladder of renditions (say 144p to 4K), cuts each into 2-6 second segments, and publishes a manifest listing them. The player measures its throughput and buffer and picks the rendition for each next segment, switching at segment boundaries. Segments are small, immutable files, so a CDN can cache them for a year.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
master.m3u8:  360p/index.m3u8   (0.8 Mbps)
              720p/index.m3u8   (2.5 Mbps)
              1080p/index.m3u8  (5 Mbps)
1080p/seg_00042.ts   <- 4-6 s, immutable, Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
  • Seek: the player jumps to the segment containing the timestamp.
  • Start-up: begin at the lowest rendition for the first 1-2 segments and step up; a shorter first segment (2 s) lowers time to first frame.
  • Format is a near one-way door: players, DRM and CDN caching rules all depend on the segment layout and manifest format.
  • Cost: a transcoding pipeline and many stored copies (the ladder is roughly 1.5-2x the source size).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Streaming bytes through your app server or API gateway.
  • Making viewers wait until all renditions finish (publish the lowest rendition first).
  • Confusing ABR with progressive download.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. HLS versus DASH? -> Both segment-based; HLS is the Apple ecosystem default, DASH is an open standard; many systems package both (CMAF can share segments, verify details).
  2. What does the player measure? -> Throughput of recent segments and buffer level; algorithms are throughput-based, buffer-based or hybrid.
  3. Why not very short segments? -> More requests and overhead; shorter segments help latency in live streams.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "multiple resolutions". The senior answer explains manifests, segment caching, start-up tuning and the one-way door of format choice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that served MP4 from an app server saw rebuffering for mobile users and huge egress bills.

questions.contextHtml: Creators upload files of up to 5 GB over mobile networks. Today the app does one PUT of the whole file to your API server. Support tickets: "upload failed at 92%, had to start over". The API servers also hit 90% CPU during the evening upload window.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Retry the upload" or "increase the timeout", still proxying bytes through the app servers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max file size? Are uploads from native apps (can chunk) or only browsers? Should we scan for malware or policy before publishing? Retention for abandoned uploads?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the gateway limits and add a per-user concurrency cap while redesigning, so evening load does not take down the API.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The failure is no resume plus proxying: a single request means a network drop restarts everything and every byte uses app CPU and bandwidth.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at the failure percentile by file size, bytes at failure, and CPU profile of the API during uploads.
  5. Root cause: One giant PUT through the app tier.
  6. Fix: Two steps. POST /v1/videos creates metadata and returns an upload session URL pointing straight at object storage (multipart upload). The client sends 8 MB chunks with Content-Range; after a failure it asks the server for the offset (Content-Range: bytes */total) and continues. Session state {videoId, totalSize, receivedBytes, uploadId} has a 7-day TTL. S3 multipart allows up to 10,000 parts of 5 MB to 5 GB each. Verify each part's checksum, assemble on completion, status moves UPLOADING -> PROCESSING -> READY | FAILED. A lifecycle rule cleans abandoned uploads after 7 days.
  7. Prevention: Metrics for upload success rate and resume rate, per-part checksum errors, orphaned multipart storage cost alert.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Chunk size: smaller means more requests, larger means more resend on failure; 8 MB is reversible per session. I would not make the API server a byte proxy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if two clients resume the same session? -> Offsets are authoritative on the server; reject out-of-order chunks.
  • How do you stop abuse? -> Authenticated session URLs with expiry and size limits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving to direct-to-storage uploads cut API CPU during the evening window from 90% to the single digits, and retries stopped producing support tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Longer timeouts.
  • Hire: Direct-to-storage, chunked, offset resume.
  • Strong hire: Session state, checksums, lifecycle cleanup and status model.

questions.promptHtml: How would you design the transcoding pipeline so a 10-minute video is ready in about a minute, and retries are safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you think about splitting work, idempotency and failure in a long-running pipeline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I don't encode a video as one job. I validate it, split it at keyframes into GOP-aligned chunks, encode each chunk for each rendition in parallel across many workers, then merge and package into HLS/DASH segments with a manifest and thumbnails. Tasks are idempotent, keyed by (videoId, rendition, chunk), so a retry is harmless. A queue delivers tasks with visibility timeouts. If a video fails three times I mark it FAILED and notify the creator.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Raw -> validate -> split at keyframes -> encode chunk x rendition (parallel) -> merge/package -> manifest + thumbs
  • Split at keyframes (GOP boundaries) so each chunk is independently decodable and segments line up.
  • 100 chunks across 100 workers turns 10 minutes of encode time per rendition into roughly 1 minute plus merge overhead.
  • Publish the lowest rendition first so the video can go live early; add higher ones as they finish.
  • Codecs: H.264 everywhere, VP9/AV1 for popular content only; audio AAC/Opus. Per-title encoding tunes the ladder per video.
  • Priority queues: short videos and popular creators first so one huge upload does not block others.
  • Worker dies: the queue re-delivers after the visibility timeout.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One monolithic transcode job per video (slow, not restartable).
  • Non-idempotent tasks, causing duplicate or corrupt output on retry.
  • No poison-video handling.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if one chunk always fails? -> After N attempts mark the video FAILED with the reason; keep the artefacts for debugging.
  2. How do you avoid visible seams? -> Keyframe-aligned chunks and consistent encoder settings.
  3. Hardware encoders? -> GPUs/ASICs cut core counts a lot; the DAG design stays.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "a queue and workers". The senior answer adds chunked parallelism, idempotency keys, rendition priority and failure handling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single-queue transcoder made a one-hour upload block short clips for hours, so the team added chunking and priorities.

questions.contextHtml: Egress is the largest line in your bill. The team proposes encoding every upload in AV1, which is much smaller than H.264 but costs far more CPU to encode (assume 10x; verify with your own benchmark). Data: 95% of videos get fewer than 100 views in their lifetime, while the top 2% account for most watch time. Many older devices lack AV1 hardware decode.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "AV1 for everything, smaller is better" or "H.264 only, simpler" without any numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What bitrate saving does AV1 give on our content (benchmark)? What share of playback devices support it? What is the egress price per GB versus the encode cost per hour?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep H.264 as the universal baseline; it is not an incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Encode cost is paid once per video; egress savings are paid per view. So AV1 pays off only for videos with many views. For a video with 50 views the extra encode never repays; for one with millions of views it does by a wide margin.
  4. How I'd verify each: Model: savings = views x GB per view x bitrate reduction x egress price versus extra encode cost. Benchmark a sample, check device support and playback failures.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The cost curve is skewed by the long tail.
  6. Fix: Always H.264 (and VP9 where supported); trigger an AV1 encode only after a video crosses a view threshold or when it is predicted to be popular (popular creators, premieres). The player picks the best supported codec from the manifest.
  7. Prevention: Track bytes served per codec, encode spend, and playback error rate by codec; revisit the threshold regularly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Storing both codecs costs space but it is reversible; renditions can be added later. I would not encode the long tail in AV1.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cold videos? -> Tier to cheaper storage classes, keep only the lowest renditions hot and re-transcode on demand.
  • Hardware encoders? -> Lower the encode cost and move the threshold down.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's AV1 pilot on the top 1% of videos recovered its encode spend within weeks, while a blanket AV1 policy would have multiplied compute for videos nobody watched.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: A blanket choice without math.
  • Hire: Views-based threshold, H.264 baseline.
  • Strong hire: Models the break-even, considers device support and cold tiering.

questions.contextHtml: The platform receives 500 hours of video per minute, average source 1080p at 8 Mbps. A rendition ladder takes about 5x the realtime work of the source, and one CPU core encodes 1080p at roughly 0.75x realtime (a benchmark to verify). The CFO asks for the daily storage, ingest bandwidth and core count.
questions.promptHtml: Do the math and call out the assumptions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Mixes up Mbps and MB/s, or counts only the raw upload and forgets the encoded ladder.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 500 h/min the peak or average? What share is long-lived (archive) versus short clips? Are hardware encoders available? Is the ladder full for every video?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a (planning).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Ingest and transcode are big but bounded; playback egress dwarfs them.
  4. How I'd verify each: Uploaded per day: 500 x 60 x 24 = 720,000 hours. 8 Mbps is 1 MB/s = 3.6 GB per hour, so about 2.6 PB/day raw. Ingest bandwidth: 2.6 PB / 86,400 s = about 30 GB/s = 240 Gbit/s. Encoded ladder about 1.5-2x the source: about 4-5 PB/day stored before tiering and dedupe. Transcode: 720k hours x 5 (ladder) = 3.6M content-hours of work per day. 3.6M / 24 = 150k hours of work per hour; at 0.75x realtime per core, about 200k cores continuously. Hardware encoders reduce this a lot.
  5. Root cause: n/a. The long tail means most of those PB are rarely read.
  6. Fix: Autoscale workers on queue age, spot or preemptible capacity for the long tail, tier old renditions to cold storage, and drop rarely used high renditions with on-demand re-transcode.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards for queue age, cores in use, cost per uploaded hour.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not provision for peak with reserved cores all day; peaks are bursty. I would not skip the ladder to save compute; viewers pay the price in rebuffering.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the peak is 3x the average? -> Queue delays are acceptable (processing can lag); autoscale and prioritise short videos.
  • What about playback egress? -> 1B hours/day at 4 Mbps (1.8 GB per hour) is about 1.8 EB/day, roughly 21 TB/s average. This is why CDNs and ISP caches exist.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A forecast that counted only raw uploads understated storage by 2x until the ladder was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Bits/bytes mix-up or only raw storage.
  • Hire: 2.6 PB/day, 30 GB/s, ladder multiplier, core estimate.
  • Strong hire: States assumptions, separates egress, proposes autoscaling and tiering.

questions.contextHtml:
After a festival, uploads triple. Creators complain that videos stay in "Processing" for hours.

transcode queue: depth 1.9M tasks   oldest task age: 5h 40m   workers: 12,000 (autoscaler max)
worker task time p50: 38 s    p99: 9 min   retries/hour: 41,000
upload service: healthy   object store: healthy
top producers: 3 channels uploading 4K 3-hour streams

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the autoscaler max" only, with no prioritisation and no look at retries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the work growing faster than capacity, or are tasks being repeated? Why 41k retries/hour? Are long jobs blocking short ones?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Separate queues or priorities so short videos and first renditions go first; publish 360p/720p early so videos become watchable; raise the cap if the budget allows (spot capacity); pause low-priority backfills.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Head-of-line blocking by 3-hour 4K jobs. (b) Retries burn capacity: workers with a visibility timeout shorter than a task's p99 get duplicates running in parallel. (c) A bad worker image. (d) Storage throttling (ruled out as healthy).
  4. How I'd verify each: Queue age by priority, task duration distribution versus the visibility timeout, retry reasons, worker logs.
  5. Root cause: Capacity cap plus long tasks and a visibility timeout shorter than the p99 task cause duplicates (9 minutes versus a 5-minute timeout, for example), amplifying load.
  6. Fix: Chunk long videos so tasks are small and uniform; set the visibility timeout above p99 and use heartbeats to extend; priority queues and fair share per creator; autoscale on queue age, not CPU; idempotent tasks so duplicates are harmless. Notify creators of expected delay.
  7. Prevention: Alert on oldest task age; load tests for festival spikes; per-tenant quotas; capacity reserved for short videos.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not drop quality renditions permanently to clear the queue. I would not kill retries globally; they protect against real failures.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a video is poison? -> After 3 failures mark FAILED and notify.
  • What about cost? -> Spot instances for low-priority work, reserved for baseline.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A timeout set at 5 minutes while p99 tasks ran 9 minutes meant a quarter of the work was done twice. Heartbeat-based extension cut the backlog in half without adding workers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only raises capacity.
  • Hire: Prioritises, finds head-of-line blocking and retry amplification.
  • Strong hire: Heartbeats, chunking, queue-age autoscaling and creator communication.

questions.contextHtml:
A video goes viral in a region that had no prior traffic. Within 3 minutes:

region sa-east: edge hit ratio 0.97 -> 0.58      origin egress: 40 Gbit/s -> 700 Gbit/s
origin object store 503 SlowDown rate: 12%      rebuffer ratio: 1.1% -> 9%
segments requested: 1080p/seg_00001..00180, same objects, from 340 edge servers

The CDN hierarchy is edge -> regional -> origin, with no shield and no request collapsing configured.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it now and structurally?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale the object store" and "add more edge servers".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the same segments requested by many edge servers at once (thundering herd)? Is the object store rate-limited per prefix? Is a shield available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn on request collapsing; route the region's misses through a shield or a nearby regional cache; temporarily serve only lower renditions (cap the top rung) to cut bytes; pre-warm the first segments.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Many edges each missing the same new objects and going to the origin independently; the object store throttling hot prefixes (503 SlowDown). Rebuffering follows from slow misses.
  4. How I'd verify each: Origin request logs show identical keys from hundreds of sources; cache status per tier; object store request metrics by prefix.
  5. Root cause: No coalescing and no shield: N edges times M objects equals N x M origin requests instead of M.
  6. Fix: Add an origin shield (the only tier that calls the origin) and enable request collapsing at every tier. Push popular new releases ahead of time (pre-position). Keep segments immutable with long TTL. Hit ratio target above 95%.
  7. Prevention: Alert on origin egress and per-key fan-in; load test a cold-region scenario; autoscale regional caches.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): An extra tier adds a hop of latency on misses, but protects the origin and is worth it. I would not just raise object store limits; the cost and risk remain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does each 1% miss matter at 100 Tbit/s? -> 1% is still 1 Tbit/s hitting lower tiers.
  • What about live manifests? -> Short TTL of 2-6 s plus collapsing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A premiere in a new market produced a 15x origin spike in minutes. A shield with collapsing turned hundreds of requests per segment into one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds capacity only.
  • Hire: Identifies herd, adds collapsing/shield, caps renditions.
  • Strong hire: Pre-positioning, cold-region test, metrics for fan-in.

questions.contextHtml:
A code review shows the play handler doing this on every view:

UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 WHERE video_id = 'v_8Hq2';

During a premiere the metrics read:

videos table: row lock wait p99 6.2 s   db cpu 35%   active connections 1,900 / 2,000
v_8Hq2 plays: 90,000 per second          playback API p99: 8 s (was 120 ms)

Metadata reads for video pages are also served from the same database.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what is the right design for counts?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index" or "add read replicas", neither of which helps a single hot row.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the count be exact and real time? Is the count shown on the page, used for monetisation, or both? Is the play path allowed to fail if counting fails?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the synchronous update from the play path (feature flag), turn it into fire-and-forget events, raise nothing else.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: All 90k writes per second serialize on one row's lock, so waits grow and connections pile up (low CPU, high lock wait confirms contention). Read replicas help reads only. An index does nothing.
  4. How I'd verify each: Lock wait views (for example pg_locks/InnoDB lock waits), connection pool saturation, a trace of the playback request.
  5. Root cause: A synchronous increment of a single hot row couples playback latency to one lock.
  6. Fix: Emit a view event to Kafka and aggregate in a stream processor every few seconds; write batched increments (for example +4,800 in one update per few seconds) to the store. Show approximate counts on the page, cached in Redis (TTL about 5 minutes for metadata). Deduplicate and validate views separately for monetisation (a separate, slower, exact pipeline). Optionally shard the counter (N sub-counters summed at read).
  7. Prevention: Load test the play path with a hot video; code review rule: no per-event writes to a shared row; alert on lock wait and pool saturation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): The cost is a few seconds of count lag and approximate numbers, which is acceptable for display; the real accounting goes through the exact pipeline. I would not couple playback availability to the analytics database.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not Redis INCR for everything? -> Fine for fast counters, but you still need durable aggregation and fraud filtering.
  • What about likes? -> Same pattern: events, aggregate, cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A premiere took playback down for 20 minutes because the view counter row was the single point of contention. Batching removed it and no one noticed the counts lagging by 3 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds index or replicas.
  • Hire: Identifies the hot row, batches via a queue.
  • Strong hire: Separates display from billing counts, shards counters, decouples play path.
